M.Sc. Thesis — Advisor Meeting — June 2026

Diachronic Interpretable Dating of Low-Resource Ancient Akkadian

A confounder-controlled benchmark, and the model that best supports automatic dating
M.Sc. Thesis · Yarin Beer · Computer Science, HUJI
Advisors: Prof. Gabriel Stanovsky  ·  Dr. Barak Sober

The thesis: a 400M translation model beats the 120B LLM — and we explain why

1 — The scholarly problem
Assyriologists date cuneiform texts by hand, leaning on ruler names, script style, and archival context — a subjective, expertise-bound, time-consuming process. For most fragments the date stays uncertain.
2 — We identify that honest dating is a chronological-ordering probing task
Year regression on a small test set inflates numbers by learning format shortcuts, not language change. We reframe: probe frozen embeddings with a deliberately weak linear model and measure Spearman rank correlation — a probe that tests whether the signal is present and decodable, not one that can overfit a tiny test set.
3 — The surprising finding
A 400M multilingual translation encoder beats the 120B LLM. Scale is flat: 1.7B → 8B → 32B → 120B all cluster near each other. Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting add nothing. The internal linear timeline reported in prior LLM work does not surface for Akkadian under linear probing.
4 — The claims (skeleton)
Mean pooling > last-token across all models. 400M > 120B. Scale is not the lever. Next-token finetuning on Akkadian is flat. The translation objective might build the diachronic signal instead of architecture, tokenizer, or finetune data alone.
The evaluation pipeline

Maximal · mean-pool · balanced · PLS · Spearman

The five-stage pipeline applied identically to every embedding source. Each step closes one dishonest shortcut. This is the reusable methodological contribution — valid for any low-resource ancient language with some dated texts.

✂
Maximal cleaning
Strip royal names, logograms, determinatives, formulae, digits. Closes: genre-format and ruler-name shortcuts.
μ
Mean pooling
Average all token hidden states into one document vector. Closes: the last-token assumption — the diachronic signal is document-level.
⚖
Balanced MC
200 Monte-Carlo draws over 8 balanced rulers, GroupKFold by ruler. Closes: majority-class imbalance and ruler leakage.
PLS
PLS projection
Extract the k≈3–5 latent directions most correlated with date. Closes: entanglement of time with genre and location.
ρ
Spearman
Score chronological ordering, not absolute year. Closes: overclaiming on a narrow span; enables fair cross-model comparison.
How the project unfolded

The experimental journey — what each phase contributed

Phase 1 — Frame the thesis & assemble the benchmark
Goal: honest, interpretable dating. Decision: probe frozen LLM activations — not text generation, not direct regression (which overfits a tiny test set). EDA found no obvious 1-D time manifold. Assembled the embedding zoo: TF-IDF, a from-scratch MLM, Qwen 1.7B/8B/32B, GPT-OSS 120B, and seq2seq encoders (base, Akkadian-only, multilingual).
Phase 2 — Make the task & data honest
Target → Spearman ordering, since fine years or 100-yr buckets overclaim on a 180-yr span. Isolated royal inscriptions to kill the style confounder. Maximal cleaning flipped TF-IDF from best to worst — proof the confounder was real. Monte-Carlo balanced 38 → 8 rulers (≥21 fragments); confirmed ordering ≠ ruler lookup.
Phase 3 — Lock the probing pipeline
Mean pooling beat last-token across the board. PLS isolated the few temporal directions across models with mismatched embedding dims. Pipeline frozen: maximal → mean → balanced MC → PLS → Spearman.
Phase 4 — Controls & tuning
Prompting (zero/few-shot, CoT) added nothing. A randomized-Qwen baseline fixed the floor. Layer scans: Thalesian peaks late, every LLM peaks early-to-middle. k = 3–5 PLS components was the sweet spot everywhere.
Phase 5 — Autopsy of the LLM paradox
Qwen recites rulers and dates in plain English yet never encodes them decodably. NTP finetuning on ORACC/EBL/Archibab: zero gain. mT5 base near the bottom. Tokenizer disproved — Thalesian fragments most yet wins. 400M multilingual ≫ 300M Akkadian-only → multilingual transfer is the lever; scale 1.7B → 120B stayed flat.
The headline result

PLS vs Ridge across all models — the 400M translation encoder wins

Key takeawayUnder the honest protocol, the 400M multilingual translation encoder achieves the highest balanced year-Spearman of every source — above all Qwen scales, the 120B model, the from-scratch MLM, and TF-IDF. PLS and Ridge agree on the ranking, so the win is not an artifact of dimensionality reduction. This is the recommended system for automatic Akkadian dating.
Where in each model does the year signal live?

Thalesian's signal deepens with layer; LLMs peak mid-network then decay

Key takeawayYear-PLS Spearman across all layers (balanced · maximal · mean). Thalesian-400M rises steadily to its best at layer 10 (★), climbing well above TF-IDF. Qwen models peak around layers 15–16 then fall back toward the baseline. The translation model concentrates its diachronic signal in late layers; LLMs peak early-to-middle and lose it.
Random-8B stays flat near 0.30 at every layer — the random floor, what the architecture gives for free before any training. Trained LLMs barely clear it.
How many dimensions does the date signal need?

k = 3–5 PLS components capture it; Ridge (dashed) confirms PLS is not cherry-picking

Key takeawaySpearman ρ vs. number of PLS components k for every model (solid lines). Most plateau between k = 3 and k = 5 — chronological information lives in a very low-dimensional subspace of the embedding. Dashed lines (Ridge, all dimensions) sit at the same level: PLS recovers the full signal with a handful of directions, not by overfitting.
Low intrinsic dimensionality is itself a finding — the chronological axis is simple once the confounders are removed.
Does scale or Akkadian finetuning help?

Scale and next-token finetuning both do nothing

Key takeawayEvery '+NTP (ft)' bar lands within noise of its untouched base model, at every scale from 1.7B to 120B — finetuning Qwen on all our Akkadian text with next-token prediction yields zero improvement. Queried in plain English, Qwen names Akkadian rulers and their dates correctly, yet that declarative knowledge never surfaces as a decodable temporal representation. The training objective is the missing ingredient, not data or parameters.
Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting also produced no gains. This is what motivates the autopsy: if not scale, data, or prompting — then what?
Autopsy: is it the tokenizer?

Thalesian wins despite the least efficient Akkadian tokenizer

Key takeawayThalesian splits Akkadian words into more subword tokens than every other model on every corpus — it is the least efficient tokenizer. GPT-OSS is most efficient (4.43 tok/word) and ranks fourth; Thalesian (6.22 tok/word) ranks first. If tokenizer quality drove performance it should lose; it wins. The tokenizer is ruled out as the cause.
Autopsy: it is the translation objective

The translation finetune alone builds a deep diachronic representation

Key takeawaySame architecture, same tokenizer, same 0.4B size — only the objective differs. Vanilla uMT5-base (red) starts at the random floor and decays below it with depth. The cuneiform translation finetune (Thalesian) builds a representation that rises to 0.41 at layer 10. Training a model to map Akkadian text to its meaning is what instils temporal structure — next-token prediction cannot.
Thalesian 0.411 vs. vanilla uMT5 0.297 → Δ = +0.114, entirely from the finetune. This is the mechanism behind the headline result.
Why the LLM cannot: the geometry of its embedding

Chronology is entangled in Qwen's embedding space, not laid out on a clean axis

Key takeawayPrior work reports a linearly-recoverable internal timeline in LLMs. For Akkadian it does not surface: the chronological signal is tangled together with genre and location, plausibly on a non-linear manifold a linear probe cannot reach.
Contributions and discussion

What we contribute, and what is missing to wrap it into a thesis

Contributions
(1) The first confounder-controlled method for dating low-resource Akkadian, cast as chronological-ordering probing. (2) A cleaned royal-inscription benchmark for Akkadian chronology (to release). (3) A benchmark across TF-IDF / MLM / Qwen 1.7–120B / multilingual seq2seq, identifying the 400M translation encoder as the recommended dating system. (4) An explanation: the prior-work LLM timeline does not surface linearly for Akkadian — accounting for why scale and prompting fail, and implicating the translation objective as what instils temporal structure.
What is missing to wrap it into a thesis — if at all?
Is the applied story — honest dating method + recommended model + “why the small model wins” explanation — already a coherent CS thesis? If not, what is the minimum still needed?
Follow-up · after the June meeting

Stress-testing the “LLMs build a linear timeline” claim on Akkadian

What we added
Six probes, each mirroring one published world-model claim on our hard regime — Gurnee–Tegmark (year), Godey (geography), “A Matter of Time” (timeline geometry), “Finding Neurons in a Haystack” (k-sparse) — plus a knowledge check and a prompting sweep. Same corpus, same frozen-activation pipeline.
The reporting standard (every slide below)
Each results slide states three lines: SETUP (text cleaning · pooling site · sampling/CV protocol), PROBE (the fitted model — PLS with k swept over {1,2,3,5}, best-k, plus a Ridge arm, unless stated otherwise), METRIC (regression → Spearman(predicted, true); classification → macro-F1 vs chance). Paired cells are always PLS / Ridge (or F1 / ρ where two metrics apply).
Are two cells actually different? (the ±std rule)
Every MC number is a mean over the SAME 200 balanced draws; the ±std (≈0.07 on mean-pool year cells, 0.2–0.4 on king-site cells) is the SD across draws, not the error of the mean. SE(mean) = std/√200 ≈ std/14, so a difference between two cells is significant (z ≥ 3) once it exceeds ≈ 0.3·std — ≥ ~0.02 for typical mean-pool cells, ≥ ~0.06–0.12 for king-site cells. All models share identical draws, so this is if anything conservative. Tool: eda/significance_mc.py (exact paired test where per-draw arrays exist — every run after 2026-07-12).
The baseline everywhere
A random-initialized Qwen3-8B pushed through the identical extraction + probing — the highlighted row in every table. Signal is “learned” only if it beats that row.
Follow-up · knowledge control

T9 — do the models know the dates? (free-text generation)

Setup
free-text generation in English, chat models only · reign-dates question: “When did {ruler} reign?” for the 8 balanced rulers → JSON {start_year, end_year} · roster question: “List the rulers of period P” → recall of the target rulers.
Probe
chat model answers; names matched diacritic-insensitively against the target rosters.
Metric
reign-window accuracy (±10 yr): correct if the answered reign window (widened by 10 yr) covers a true reign year · kings recall: fraction of the period’s target rulers the model names, scored on the raw text (normalized substrings; robust to truncation and spelling variants).

Stress test · geometry-aware probes (working note §2)

P9 — geodesic kernel PLS: does the manifold’s curvature help?

Setup
mean pool, rows L2-normalized (distances = Euclidean on unit vectors ≡ cosine ranking) · Akkadian maximal + English tier0 (other cleanings in the CSV) · 8-ruler balanced MC, GroupKFold-by-ruler · k=10 NN graph per training fold; out-of-sample through the fixed train graph (no leakage).
Probe
G-KPLS: kernel PLS on the geodesic Gram KG = −½HD²H (Isomap’s kernel; D = graph-geodesic distances), components a ∈ {1,2,3,5} best-a · RBF-KPLS: identical KPLS on the Euclidean RBF kernel, median-heuristic bandwidth — isolates curvature vs kernel · KRR-on-KG: kernel ridge, λ ∈ {.001, .01, .1} — isolates PLS vs kernel.
Metric
Spearman(predicted year, true), best layer per cell; columns per cleaning = G-KPLS | a | RBF-KPLS | a | KRR, where a = the chosen number of KPLS components (grid {1,2,3,5}). λ exists ONLY for the KRR arm (grid {.001, .01, .1}) — it picked 0.1 in every cell, TF-IDF included; G-KPLS and RBF-KPLS have no λ, their only hyper is a. PLS ref = the plain linear probe on the same cleaning (P1 / translation slides).

Stress test · geometry-aware probes (working note §4)

P8 — the supervision dial: how much supervision does chronology need?

Setup
one vector per fragment (average of its token activations, length-normalized) · same 200 balanced draws, train/test split by ruler — the probe never sees the test kings.
Probe
ONE probe with a knob λ that mixes two goals. λ=0: “find the direction that best matches the YEAR” (fully supervised, like supervised PCA). λ=1: “find the direction along which similar texts stay close” — pure shape of the point cloud, the year is never used (Laplacian eigenmaps). In-between λ = weighted mix of the two goals (solved as a single eigenproblem, [(1−λ)HKyH − λL]z = γDz, on PCA-100 features; test fragments are projected linearly — no leakage). NOT the KPLS family: no components “a” and no kernel choice here — the only RBF is inside Ky, the similarity of the YEAR LABELS in the supervised term.
Metric
|Spearman| between the probe’s 1st coordinate and the true year, on held-out rulers. How to read it: if the λ=1 column (year never used) matches λ=0, the year-ordering is already in the cloud’s shape; if λ=0 wins, supervision has to dig it out. ★ = row best. Akkadian shown name-stripped (maximal); tier0/maxking in the CSV.

Stress test · forced behavioral dating

T12 — ask the LLM: the answer replaces the activation probe

Setup
each fragment is shown to the chat model under the four T10 prompt styles (bare / expert / few-shot k=5, leakage-free pool / CoT) and the model’s generated answer (ruler + year_bce, forced single best guess) is the prediction — the behavioral counterpart of probing the prompted activations (T10) · greedy · same parse ladder + [1,2000] BCE gate.
Probe
none — the ANSWER is the prediction; scored on the same 200 balanced draws. Ruler names parsed and normalized to the canonical 8.
Metric
top table: Spearman(answered year, true) on the 200 shared draws · bottom table: ruler macro-F1 over the 8 canonical rulers (missing/wrong names count as misses). tier0 (name-confounded) columns retired to the CSV.

External validation · Gurnee & Tegmark 2023

Our models do represent space & time — on English

Setup
the “world models” protocol on six English datasets (3 spatial → lat/lon, 3 temporal → year): each entity’s last-token embedding per layer → ridge probe on held-out entities. Our ladder, plus the paper’s Llama-2 and a random-init control the paper never ran.

best-layer held-out test R². A score witnesses learning only if it beats BOTH the TF-IDF floor and its own random-init twin.

TF-IDF is a real floor (.642 world; it even wins NYC): trained models clear it, random arms fall below. The small translation encoders (cunei / AKK-300M) sit near the floor on English. * = control.

Layer sweep · Gurnee & Tegmark protocol

English — where in the network do space & time live?

Setup
Per-layer ridge probe over all six English datasets, plotted against normalized depth (layer / n_layers) so ladders with 28–41 layers are comparable. TIME = Spearman, SPACE = R² (symlog, so the negative tail compresses and the 0–1 band stays readable). Left = last token (paper-faithful), right = mean pool (ours). Colours by family: Qwen blues, Llama greens, encoders orange/purple, darker = larger. Dashed = random-init controls. ★ marks each arm’s maximum.
Key takeawaySignal rises to a mid/late-depth peak then decays for every trained arm — the world model is built in the middle of the network, not at the output. The random-init arms stay flat at the bottom in both space and time, so the geometry is learned rather than architectural. gpt-oss-120B (darkest blue) lands mid-pack, below the Llama ladder despite being the largest model — scale alone does not buy a better world model.
Dimensionality · best layer

English — how many PLS components does the world model need?

Setup
At each arm’s best layer, PLS with k = 1…64 components. Same metrics (TIME = Spearman, SPACE = R²), same colour scheme, both poolings. ★ = the k that maximises the score.
Key takeawayTrained arms keep gaining up to k ≈ 8–16, while the random-init controls saturate by k ≈ 3–5. The learned representation is genuinely higher-dimensional, not merely stronger along one axis — a distinction the single-number R² tables hide. Space needs more components than time, consistent with lat/lon being a genuinely 2-D target.
Layer sweep · the Akkadian mirror

Akkadian — the same layer analysis on our corpus

Setup
Identical protocol on the Akkadian fragments: YEAR = Spearman, GEO = R² (symlog), for both text variants — akk_maximal (raw Akkadian) and eng_tier0 (the faithful literal gloss; the hallucinating eng_maximal clean is excluded). Both poolings shown; the three encoders appear only in the mean panels (no causal last token). gpt-oss-120B now included. ★ = maximum.
Key takeawayThe English shape does not reproduce: curves are flatter, peaks are weaker, and the trained arms sit on top of their random twins rather than far above them. The small translation encoders (cuneiform-400M, AKK-300M, orange) are competitive with — often above — the largest LLMs on Akkadian, which is the thesis’s central inversion seen layer-by-layer.
Dimensionality · the Akkadian mirror

Akkadian — PLS components at the best layer

Setup
Best-layer PLS sweep, k = 1…64, on both Akkadian text variants and both poolings. Same metrics and colours as the English PLS slide. ★ = best k.
Key takeawayOn Akkadian the trained-vs-random separation in k largely disappears: most arms peak around k ≈ 3–8 and the encoders are compact and low-rank. Combined with the flat layer curves, this says the Akkadian “signal” is a shallow, low-dimensional surface feature (king-name strings), not the rich multi-component geometry the same probes find in English.
